summary: Dexamethasone is a potent, long-acting synthetic glucocorticoid used for its anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects across many organ systems - allergic, dermatologic, endocrine, GI, hematologic, neoplastic, neurologic, ophthalmic, renal, respiratory, and rheumatic disorders - and in diagnostic suppression testing. At equipotent anti-inflammatory doses it almost completely lacks the sodium-retaining (mineralocorticoid) activity of hydrocortisone (1.5 mg dexamethasone equals about 40 mg hydrocortisone). Dose is highly individualized (0.75-9 mg/day orally) and must be tapered after prolonged use to avoid adrenal insufficiency. Key risks include increased susceptibility to and masking of infections, HPA-axis/adrenal suppression, hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, GI ulceration/perforation, and neuropsychiatric effects.
indications: Allergic states (severe asthma, atopic/contact dermatitis, drug hypersensitivity, allergic rhinitis, serum sickness)
Dermatologic diseases (pemphigus, severe erythema multiforme/Stevens-Johnson, exfoliative erythroderma)
Endocrine disorders (adrenocortical insufficiency, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, hypercalcemia of cancer, nonsuppurative thyroiditis)
Gastrointestinal diseases (regional enteritis, ulcerative colitis - critical periods)
Hematologic disorders (autoimmune hemolytic anemia, ITP, pure red cell aplasia)
Neoplastic diseases (palliative management of leukemias and lymphomas)
Nervous system (cerebral edema, acute MS exacerbations)
Ophthalmic, renal (idiopathic nephrotic syndrome), respiratory (sarcoidosis, berylliosis), and rheumatic disorders
Diagnostic testing of adrenocortical hyperfunction (dexamethasone suppression test)

moa: Dexamethasone is a synthetic adrenocortical glucocorticoid that is readily absorbed from the GI tract. Glucocorticoids cause varied metabolic effects and modify the body's immune responses to diverse stimuli; dexamethasone is used primarily for potent anti-inflammatory effects across many organ systems. At equipotent anti-inflammatory doses it almost completely lacks the sodium-retaining property of hydrocortisone. It acts as a corticosteroid hormone receptor agonist and is a moderate inducer of CYP3A4.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to the product or its constituents
Administration of live/live-attenuated vaccines during immunosuppressive doses
relative: Active or latent peptic ulcer, diverticulitis, fresh intestinal anastomoses, ulcerative colitis (perforation risk)
Congestive heart failure, hypertension, renal insufficiency
Myasthenia gravis or neuromuscular-blocker use (acute myopathy)
Recent myocardial infarction (left ventricular free-wall rupture)
monitor: Intraocular pressure if therapy exceeds 6 weeks
Patients exposed to chickenpox or measles

preg: Pregnancy Category C. Corticosteroids are teratogenic in many species at human-equivalent doses, with increased cleft palate in offspring of treated mice, rats, and rabbits. There are no adequate well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus, and observe infants of mothers who received substantial doses for signs of hypoadrenalism.
lact: Systemically administered corticosteroids appear in human milk and could suppress growth, interfere with endogenous corticosteroid production, or cause other untoward effects. Decide whether to discontinue nursing or the drug, taking into account the importance of the drug to the mother.
renal: Sodium and fluid retention with potassium loss can occur, so use with caution in renal insufficiency. Average and large doses can elevate blood pressure and cause sodium/water retention; dietary salt restriction and potassium supplementation may be needed.
hepatic: There is an enhanced corticosteroid effect in patients with cirrhosis due to decreased metabolism. Metabolic clearance is also affected by thyroid status. Use caution and consider lower doses.

major: CYP3A4 inducers (barbiturates, phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampin) - enhance metabolism; may need higher corticosteroid dose
CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, macrolides such as erythromycin) - raise corticosteroid levels and side-effect risk
Live/attenuated vaccines - contraindicated at immunosuppressive doses; diminished response to all vaccines/toxoids
Anticholinesterases - severe weakness in myasthenia gravis
moderate: Antidiabetic agents - corticosteroids raise blood glucose; may need dose adjustment
Oral anticoagulants (warfarin) - usually inhibited response; monitor coagulation
Potassium-depleting agents (amphotericin B, diuretics) - hypokalemia; amphotericin B plus corticosteroid linked to cardiac enlargement/CHF
Cyclosporine - increased activity of both; convulsions reported
Estrogens/oral contraceptives - decreased hepatic metabolism, increased corticosteroid effect
Phenytoin - both increases and decreases in levels reported
minor: Aminoglutethimide - may diminish corticosteroid-induced adrenal suppression
Isoniazid - serum concentrations may be decreased
interactions.food: Take with food to reduce GI upset; dietary salt restriction and potassium supplementation may be needed.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid or limit; combination with NSAIDs/alcohol increases GI ulcer and bleeding risk.
interactions.diagnostics: May suppress reactions to skin tests; indomethacin can cause false-negative dexamethasone suppression tests; can raise glucose and lower potassium.

common: Cushingoid features (moon face, abnormal fat deposits)
serious: Decreased resistance to infection and masking of infection
Peptic ulcer with possible perforation and hemorrhage
Posterior subcapsular cataracts, glaucoma, increased IOP
rare: Pseudotumor cerebri (increased intracranial pressure, usually after discontinuation)

monitoring: Blood pressure, weight, and fluid/electrolyte status
Signs of infection (corticosteroids may mask them)
Intraocular pressure if therapy continues beyond 6 weeks
Bone mineral density and fracture risk on prolonged therapy
Growth velocity, blood pressure, IOP, and infection in pediatric patients
Adrenal function and stress-dosing needs during tapering
counsel: Do not stop the medicine abruptly or without medical supervision
Carry information that you are taking a corticosteroid and seek care promptly for fever or signs of infection
Avoid exposure to chickenpox or measles; seek medical advice promptly if exposed
Take with food; report black/tarry stools, severe abdominal pain, or vision changes
Report mood changes, muscle weakness, or swelling
Tell all providers you take corticosteroids, especially before surgery or vaccination
pk: Readily absorbed from the GI tract; cerebral-edema response usually within 12-24 hours
Long-acting glucocorticoid (biologic effect persists ~36-54 h; not stated on this label)
Long-acting; dosed once daily or less often for many indications
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); protect from moisture; light-resistant container
pearls: 1.5 mg dexamethasone is roughly equivalent to 40 mg hydrocortisone, 10 mg prednisone, or 8 mg methylprednisolone (oral/IV)
Almost no mineralocorticoid (sodium-retaining) activity at anti-inflammatory doses
Always taper after prolonged therapy - HPA-axis suppression can persist for months
Increase the dose during stress, illness, surgery, or trauma to prevent adrenal crisis
Can mask infection and reactivate latent TB, Strongyloides, or amebiasis - screen before chronic use
Dexamethasone is a moderate CYP3A4 inducer and may lower levels of CYP3A4 substrates
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip it and resume the usual schedule - do not double up. Never stop the medicine on your own, since prolonged use makes patients dependent on corticosteroids and abrupt withdrawal can cause adrenal insufficiency.
overdose: Treatment of overdosage is by supportive and symptomatic therapy. In acute overdosage, depending on the patient's condition, supportive measures may include gastric lavage or emesis.
